review:
Okay, to start off, I really think this game is awesome. It's got an interesting premise and a great atmosphere.

However, in it's current state, it feels a little... lacking in some of the plot elements, especially towards the end. It is also a short game, and a little pricey for the length.

BUT, I believe that the potential in this game is very high, and that is what keeps me closely invested in this game's development.

I just can't recommend Strobophagia to the [u]average[/u] player at it's current stage. I'm leaving a negative review because I don't want the average player to have a bad time because the game didn't live up to their expectations. I will update this review(or make a new one) once the game gets smoothed out a little bit.

Keep up the good work, devs.

By far one of the trippier games to play. Full of seizure inducing light shows and awesome music, you get to drink beer and smack other party goers around until one of them turns around to finally knock you down a peg. Then you get back by cracking a beer bottle across the head to knock them out for a few.

Meanwhile, you're busy completing the rites so that you can eventually free some entity so they can see the world through your eyes. 

In other words, go play this!
Played almost 2 hours, then got stuck in the floor and couldn't reload to fix. As well as during the play I had to restard game to fix sprinting. Not currently playable

It really pains me to not recommend this since I enjoyed the alpha, but this has way too many issues right now. I spent more time being frustrated and lost than scared while playing. 

I think this game has a lot of potential and I hope it reaches it.

Absolutely amazing in every aspect,  the devs are hardworking and did a wonderful job creating a rave like atmosphere while maintaining a scary and on edge vibe. The sound track is great with pulse pounding edm contrasted with stark earie silence. And the best for last the Absolutely stunning and trippy beautiful visuals. For 20 bucks this game is a psychedelic steal. Recommended 10/10

The aesthetic and the soundtrack to this game is simply fantastic, definitely very unique. Have stalled progressing the story just to listen to the tracks playing before. The character movement feels decent and the puzzles involved are fun. You use a phone picked up at the beginning of the game which is vital to continuing the plot. While other games may solely use them as a light source, this game allows you to read messages from other ravers, take photos and pick up new signals around the maps. Personally found this quite entertaining and a bit different from some other games I have played in the past.

There are some issues though, the plot has very little sustenance in an occult sense. The Aleister Crowley influences are apparent but shallow, and the ending was basically an information dump that didn't really feel that satisfying. It felt rushed instead. The game is also very short for the price. 

Overall I would recommend this game from an incredibly biased and shallow perspective; the visuals are a treat as is the soundtrack. The character movement and phone interactions were nice as well.

As someone who loves drugs, festivals, and video games I had much higher hopes for this game because the premise is unique. For a game that deals with "raves", there is a distinct lack of music in this game. Maybe 3 or 4 songs but none of them really give you that rave feels. There was one really cool and unique idea where you had to follow the music to get out of a maze, but that's about it. 
The game doesn't run very well and it's kind of clunky. 

You have a phone the entire time but you don't have the option to use the light on the phone. Also you don't really need to use the phone very much to progress through the game. You need it for maybe a few parts but then it stops playing an importance later on. 

I'll buy this game again if they keep improving it, but to me it seems like they released an unfinished project

[i]This is the [b]12th[/b] review of the Steam Redlight series, a series where I purposely seek out negatively or controversially rated games on Steam to see if they're as bad as the Internet says they are. It's accompanied by a video review that can be found [b][url=https://youtu.be/5i0D1ROPeG8]here[/url][/b].[/i]

[b]In summary, I cannot recommend this game[/b], while the game is easy on the eyes (unless you suffer photosensitivity), it lacks in most other categories such as depth, plot progression, and even overall scare and atmosphere. The game is an amazing visual product, but doesn’t make for a great game, horror or otherwise.
[h2] Introduction [/h2]
In Strobophagia, you play as a nameless faceless forest-rave attendee with hundreds if not a thousand others. At this rave, you rely on a cell phone that’s provided to you to stay in contact with the organizers, the attendees, and even [i]something else[/i]. With this cell phone, you’ll connect to local reception networks to interact with the residents of that space. For the most part, this cell phone acts as your compass, camera, and context, but does little more than that. Also, you can’t use the phone’s flashlight in this game.

Strobophagia is a short first-person visually-motivated horror game. You’ll experience a woodland rave where you’ll encounter the [i]others[/i] which will slowly educate you on what’s really happening here. This game works in four self-dubbed chapters, one being the tutorial, the second being where you learn of your role in this gathering, the third is a crescendo event that emphasizes [i]the others’[/i] presence, and then the fourth is a reconciliation of the games’ themes.  It’s hard to say what the actual play time of this game is, but an hour and a half might be a good estimate depending on your ability to solve riddles and puzzles. For myself, I completed the game in roughly forty minutes in one playthrough, but that was after restarting and skipping the tutorial portion of the game.

[b]My descriptions of what I liked and disliked may spoil some story elements, so please discontinue if you want to preserve your knowledge of the game to as little as possible.[/b]
[h2] The Good [/h2]
It goes without saying that the strongest part of this game is its visual representations. It holds a unique theme that I haven’t really seen reproduced in gaming. While some of the animations can look a little stiff or abnormal, the whole game is essentially one-long acid trip, so I think the animations can honestly play out however they want.

Another thing that I did enjoy is the overall plot device of the game -- the presence of [i]the others[/i] is not one that I commonly will see in games. The unique visuals combined with the uncommon occult influences really do tee this game up to being a unique experience, if only...
[h2] The Bad [/h2]
...things were given a little more depth. Earlier, I said that this game was short, and it realistically is. It’s hard to say how much extra-curricular content there actually is to explore aside from my understanding of there being at least two endings, but the exposure you’re given during the gameplay which seems mostly linear is water-driplike. In my specific ending, you’re essentially just hamfisted most of the explanations, such as how the party started, why the organizers wear bird masks, who are [i]the others[/i] and etc., but even though you spend seven minutes or so reading that whole exchange, there’s still a lot left to wonder. You encounter some pretty significant characters that don’t really seem to get their place in the story like Phix, Ami, or Hedonis even though they impact the game in some pretty large ways. The influence of this game was lined up to provide a strong experience, but I feel like this wasn’t done justice within the small window of time the game takes.

Another thing that bothered me was the overall threat of the game. During my playthrough, I encountered two enemies -- the faceless husks and the horned beast. The faceless husks appear in the forest, but they can just be slapped away, I kid you not. They walk up, you hit them, empty handed, and they run off. I defended myself from three of them as I went from point-to-point and was not the slightest bit intimidated by their presence. For the horned beast, they run faster than you when they catch you, so if you happen to get spotted by them you can just lay down and die. There’s no tense cat-and-mouse chase, nor is there much difficulty in avoiding the beast in the mazes, and to round it all off the mazes are pretty short, so your encounter with the beast isn’t given adequate time to foster feelings of fear. Even things that may have been intended to have been well-placed or deserved jumpscares didn’t get a response because I was either frustrated with other parts of the game [i]or[/i] the atmosphere didn’t match to get the reaction it was aiming for.

A point I had made earlier that I wanted to essentially reiterate because it bothered me so much is really the length of the game. My playtime is about two hours in total, with the extra being mostly non-gameplay related. Within those two hours, I spent the first forty or so minutes in the tutorial trying to get past Oedipa’s task, but after frustrating myself with it I just decided to go find the next control box on my own. On top of those forty minutes, I experienced probably thirty minutes of gameplay before being forced to reload my game due to a bug. Thankfully, the game allows you to essentially bypass the tutorial and go straight to the last checkpoint so you can begin the second chapter -- this means that of those two hours, I only really spent forty minutes playing the remainder of the game. The amount of gameplay stored in the game seems pretty negligible for its heavy price tag of $20 USD. This does leave me conflicted, because the art assets are gorgeous and should be worth the weight of its tag, but with everything else falling short in terms of gameplay, story, atmosphere, and even music -- because I spent a good amount of time mostly in silence in this game, the visuals aren’t enough to prop the game’s value up. Everything in this game is further diminished by the need to restart it due to bugs, which brings me up to my last point.

During my time, I experienced at least two bugs -- one game breaking, and one deceivingly inconvenient bug. The first I had encountered was during Phix’s riddle -- I was no longer able to see messages on my phone. This posed a significant challenge because I [i]couldn’t remember what Phix’s riddle was[/i] and had nothing to reference. I thought this was sort of a punishment for failing the riddle earlier, but I soon understood that the game was broken when I couldn’t interact with environmental elements such as putting things into containers. When I reloaded the game, I was dropped into what could have been an infinite loading screen in the intro cutscene right before I got my phone. It took me about three minutes before realizing I could press “Escape” to leave this loading screen, and on a further reload I was given another faux-loading screen when dropping into the dream-intro scene. Since the game is short, I didn’t have to redo a lot of my progress since I could bypass the tutorial, but it does take heavy points away from the atmosphere and flow of the game when you have to retrace your steps.

Also, I don’t quite know why I can’t drink the wine but I [b]can[/b] drink the beer. Just something I wonder about sometimes while thinking about this game.
[h2] The End [/h2]
Anyway, that’s all the text that we have room for. Game’s [b]ok[/b], it’s just not a very satisfying experience.

Strobophagia | Rave Horror, developed by Green Tile Digital and published by Green Tile Digital alongside THQ Nordic, is a strikingly unconventional horror experience that deliberately breaks away from the genre’s usual darkness and restraint. Instead of abandoned houses, hospitals, or fog-filled streets, the game drops players into a surreal rave festival deep in the forest, where pulsing neon lights, masked dancers, and electronic music form the backdrop for an unsettling descent into the unknown. From the very beginning, the game establishes itself as something different—horror not born from silence and shadows alone, but from overstimulation, disorientation, and the creeping realization that the celebration itself is hiding something deeply sinister.

The narrative is presented in an intentionally fragmented and mysterious way. You arrive at the so-called Headless Rave Festival with little context, guided by cryptic messages and vague instructions delivered through your in-game smartphone. As you explore, it becomes increasingly clear that the festival is more than a party; it is tied to an ancient, ritualistic presence that feeds on participation and attention. Storytelling unfolds subtly through environmental details, text messages, symbols, and conversations, leaving players to piece together meaning rather than spelling everything out directly. This approach reinforces the game’s dreamlike tone, making the plot feel more like a disturbing urban legend than a traditional horror narrative.

Gameplay focuses almost entirely on exploration and puzzle-solving rather than combat. There are no weapons or direct means of defense, which shifts the tension toward awareness and navigation. The smartphone plays a central role, acting as both a narrative device and a gameplay tool. By tracking Wi-Fi signals scattered throughout the festival grounds, players are guided toward points of interest, puzzles, and story progression. This mechanic gives the experience a scavenger-hunt feel, encouraging curiosity while also creating unease as signals draw you deeper into unfamiliar and increasingly disturbing areas. Occasional threats and hostile encounters force you to rely on movement and quick thinking rather than confrontation, heightening vulnerability.

Visually, Strobophagia is one of its strongest offerings. The game embraces a psychedelic aesthetic filled with glowing colors, exaggerated costumes, towering statues, and dynamic lighting that constantly shifts the mood. The rave environment is dense with visual stimuli, creating a sense of sensory overload that mirrors the themes of excess and loss of control. This visual intensity makes the horror feel surreal rather than grounded, blurring the line between reality and hallucination. The contrast between lively dance areas and darker, more ominous forest paths sustains tension, as players are never quite sure where danger may emerge.

Sound design and music play a crucial role in shaping the experience, though their effectiveness can vary. Electronic and rave-inspired tracks fit the setting and help establish immersion, especially during moments of exploration among crowds. However, the audio landscape sometimes struggles to maintain consistent intensity, with certain sections feeling quieter or less impactful than expected. While the music reinforces the theme, it does not always fully capitalize on opportunities to amplify fear or tension, occasionally leaving moments that feel emotionally underpowered despite strong visuals.

The pacing of the game is relatively short and focused, with a single playthrough typically lasting only a few hours. This brevity makes the experience feel more like a concentrated horror vignette than a full-length adventure. Multiple endings and hidden narrative elements offer some replay value, particularly for players interested in uncovering every detail or exploring alternate outcomes. Still, the compact structure means that Strobophagia leaves a stronger impression through atmosphere and concept than through mechanical depth or long-term engagement.

Technical execution is functional but not flawless. While the game generally runs as intended, minor bugs, unclear objectives, and occasional navigation confusion can interrupt immersion. These rough edges are noticeable, especially in a title that relies heavily on atmosphere and player engagement. That said, the artistic ambition often compensates for these shortcomings, and many players are willing to forgive technical imperfections in exchange for such a distinctive experience.

Ultimately, Strobophagia | Rave Horror is best understood as an experimental blend of horror, art installation, and interactive narrative. It does not rely on jump scares or traditional survival mechanics, instead cultivating dread through symbolism, overstimulation, and uncertainty. Its strengths lie in its visual identity, thematic originality, and willingness to explore horror through an unconventional lens. While its short length, uneven audio, and limited mechanical complexity may prevent it from appealing to everyone, it stands out as a memorable and daring entry in the indie horror space. For players seeking a horror experience that feels strange, hypnotic, and unlike anything else on Steam, Strobophagia offers a haunting journey into a rave where the music never truly stops—and neither does the sense that something is terribly wrong.

Rating: 7/10

A great addition to today's gaming libraries, Strobophagia was a really interesting experience. While not quite a walking sim, it still kept gameplay to a minimum to focus on the story at hand. With the unique gameplay of signals and connection, this rave style festival game is honestly a work of art to experience. The atmosphere was brisk and engaging, while still being mostly linear and simple to follow. An easy going exploration horror experience, with some quick paced gameplay at the end of the run to keep things interesting.
For stylization alone I would recommend it. One of the most creative art styles in a sequence to actually add to the gameplay style, this game felt like an actual festival. While the story felt limited, the way in which it was told brought the narrative together that makes up for loose threads. All and all, a must play through experience.

UFFDA UUUUFFFFDA I guess 7 times the charm to beat this game! I had this game bug out forcing me to restart so many times that I became a pro speed runner at it. The movement has that walking on ice feel mixed in with the walking through sand feel. When moving the mouse back and forth you'll get a bit of a drift like you built up momentum which is an odd feeling but you strafe back and forth really slow and come to a weird dead stop when running. It's really hard to explain but imagine the upper half of your body sliding down an icy hill while the lower half of your body is trying to climb out of mud.

I get that the game has a RAVE theme but it should also have a SEIZURE warning theme. The bright lights and music aren't what will get you it will be the random screeching loud scream mixed in with a bunch of different color filters that will send you into cardiac arrest. There is more than one time where the game goes a little over the time with the effects. 

With ALOT of polish and a few tweaks I would honestly say this game might be worth 20$ but for now I'd pass it up.
